question:
Patient note:
A 55-year-old woman, originally right-hand dominant but now reliant on her left hand for most tasks, arrived to the general medicine clinic accompanied by her partner for a scheduled comprehensive review of her chronic conditions and new concerns of intermittent right-leg spasticity that has made transfers from bed to wheelchair more difficult during the past month. Eighteen months earlier she suffered an acute ischemic event involving the left middle cerebral artery territory, confirmed by diffusion-weighted MRI, for which she received intravenous alteplase within the therapeutic window; mechanical thrombectomy was not required. She completed a five-week inpatient rehabilitation program followed by extensive outpatient physical and occupational therapy. Despite excellent engagement, she retains dense weakness of the right upper extremity and only antigravity strength in the right lower extremity; she propels herself in a lightweight wheelchair for community distances and uses a quad-cane to ambulate short indoor stretches. Speech is fluent and comprehension intact, and she has resumed remote bookkeeping work without difficulty remembering passwords, preparing spreadsheets, or managing deadlines, which her partner corroborates. She has never experienced an episode of decompensated pump failure—there have been no hospital encounters for pulmonary congestion, orthopnea, or lower-extremity edema—and she recalls no episodes of crushing chest pressure, diaphoresis, or urgent catheterization suggestive of coronary occlusion, and no clinician has ever documented a myocardial infarction. She has no personal history of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, asthma, or other chronic lung conditions, and spirometry performed as part of a preoperative evaluation last year showed normal flows and volumes. She has never been diagnosed with autoimmune connective tissue disorders such as rheumatoid arthritis, systemic lupus erythematosus, systemic sclerosis, or polymyositis. Her most recent HIV antigen/antibody screen, performed within the past year, was negative, and she has no history of opportunistic infections. Approximately five years ago she was informed of chronically mildly elevated aminotransferases; further work-up revealed hepatitis C antibody positivity with low-level viremia. A staging vibration-controlled transient elastography at that time yielded a liver stiffness measurement of 6.0 kPa, and laboratory studies have consistently demonstrated preserved synthetic capacity—albumin this visit 3.8 g/dL, international normalized ratio 1.1, and platelet count 210 × 10⁹/L. Abdominal ultrasound performed six months ago demonstrated a smooth hepatic outline without nodularity, splenomegaly, or fluid accumulation, and she has never developed jaundice, ascites, encephalopathy, or variceal bleeding. Screening colonoscopy at age 50 revealed only small hyperplastic polyps, and a recent low-dose chest CT ordered because of a remote 10-pack-year smoking history (quit age 30) was unremarkable. Fasting glucose measurements over the past three years have fluctuated between 100 and 112 mg/dL; she adheres to a Mediterranean diet, and her most recent hemoglobin A1c, drawn two weeks ago, was 5.8 %. She does not take metformin or other glycemic agents. Renal function has remained stable with serum creatinine 0.8 mg/dL and estimated glomerular filtration rate 92 mL/min/1.73 m²; urinalysis today is negative for protein or blood. She has never been diagnosed with hematologic or solid organ malignancies, has had no abnormal lymphadenopathy, and age-appropriate cervical cancer screening last year was negative. Current medications include aspirin 81 mg daily, clopidogrel 75 mg daily started after the cerebrovascular event, atorvastatin 40 mg nightly, baclofen 10 mg three times daily for tone control, and vitamin D 1000 IU per day; she uses no herbal supplements, alcohol intake is limited to a glass of wine twice monthly, and she denies illicit drug use. Vital signs in clinic: temperature 36.7 °C, blood pressure 118/72 mm Hg seated, heart rate 74 beats per minute and regular, respiratory rate 14 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 98 % breathing room air. Body mass index is 23 kg/m². Neurologic examination reveals expressive language intact, cranial nerves II–XII normal, right upper limb strength 1/5 in proximal and distal muscle groups, right lower limb strength 3/5 with spastic catch at the ankle, brisk deep tendon reflexes on the right with sustained clonus at the Achilles, and an upgoing plantar response; sensation to light touch and pinprick is preserved bilaterally. Left extremities show full strength and tone. Cardiovascular exam discloses a regular rhythm without murmurs, gallops, or rubs, and jugular venous pulsation is not elevated. Lungs are clear to auscultation with vesicular breath sounds throughout. The abdomen is soft, nontender, and without hepatomegaly or shifting dullness; a faint spider angioma is noted on the upper chest. No peripheral edema is present. Basic laboratory panel collected this morning shows hemoglobin 13.6 g/dL, white blood cell count 6.4 × 10⁹/L, sodium 139 mmol/L, potassium 4.1 mmol/L, bicarbonate 25 mmol/L, blood urea nitrogen 14 mg/dL, AST 68 U/L, ALT 72 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 102 U/L, total bilirubin 1.2 mg/dL, and glucose 108 mg/dL. Twelve-lead electrocardiogram demonstrates normal sinus rhythm at 72 beats per minute with normal intervals and no Q-waves or ST-T abnormalities. A non-contrast head CT performed earlier in the week after a minor unwitnessed fall shows the expected left-sided encephalomalacia without new hemorrhage or infarct. The patient seeks guidance on adjusting antispasmodic therapy and reviewing secondary stroke prevention while monitoring her chronic viral hepatitis, glucose trends, and lipid profile.

Question: What is the patient's Charlson Comorbidity Index (CCI)? You should use the patient's medical values and health status when they were first admitted to the hospital prior to any treatment.
solution:
Age-adjusted Charlson Comorbidity Index (CCI), scoring cerebrovascular disease and hemiplegia as separate items:
- Age 55 (50–59 years): 1 point.
- Cerebrovascular disease: prior imaging-confirmed left middle cerebral artery ischemic stroke = 1 point.
- Hemiplegia/hemiparesis: persistent severe right-sided motor impairment after the stroke, with arm strength 1/5 and leg strength 3/5 = 2 points.
- Mild liver disease: chronic hepatitis C with preserved synthetic function and no portal hypertension or decompensation = 1 point.
- Other CCI conditions: 0. A1c 5.8% does not establish diabetes. There is no documented myocardial infarction, heart failure, peripheral vascular disease, dementia, chronic lung disease, connective tissue disease, peptic ulcer, significant renal disease, malignancy, or AIDS.
Total = 1 + 1 + 2 + 1 = 5.
Final answer: 5
